en: Existing as an idea rather than a physical thing; not concrete
hook: ABSTRACT: pulled away (abs-tract) from the physical world.
story: Abstract. In philosophy class, Rafi's teacher asked, 'What is justice?' Rafi pointed out of the window at the court building. 'That is a building,' the teacher said. 'I asked about justice itself.' Justice, freedom and beauty are abstract: existing as ideas rather than physical things. You cannot touch them or put them in a bag. The opposite is concrete. Abstract art shows shapes and colours rather than recognizable objects. Synonyms: theoretical, conceptual, intangible.

gre.s: The professor's lectures were so ____ that students begged for concrete examples, unable to connect her elegant theories to anything in the real world.
gre.clue: students begged for concrete examples

example: Mahbub found economics too abstract until a summer job at his uncle's rice mill showed him supply and demand in action.

en: Reachable or usable without difficulty; also, easy to understand
hook: ACCESSIBLE: easy ACCESS.
story: Accessible. Professor Kamal's first physics lectures were full of equations nobody could follow. After a dismal midterm, he changed his style. He explained gravity with a falling mango and electricity with the classroom ceiling fan. Suddenly even the history students taking his course as an elective understood him. His lectures had become accessible: easy to reach, use, or understand. A building with ramps is accessible to wheelchair users. Think: access is a way in, and accessible means there is a way in.

gre.s: Unlike his dense earlier treatises, which only specialists could follow, the philosopher's final book is remarkably ____, written in plain prose for a general audience.
gre.clue: written in plain prose for a general audience

example: Shahana's science podcast makes genetics accessible to teenagers by explaining each idea through a simple kitchen experiment.

en: A public supporter of a cause; to argue publicly in its favor
hook: ADVOCATE: in Bangladesh, a lawyer is literally called an 'advocate', someone who speaks FOR you.
story: Advocate. After her cousin was hit by a speeding bus outside his school, Nadia could not stay quiet. She spoke at assemblies, wrote letters to newspapers, and stood outside the city office every Friday with a sign. Within a year, the school had a zebra crossing and a speed bump. Nadia had become an advocate: someone who publicly supports a cause. As a verb, to advocate means to argue in favour of something. In Bangladesh, lawyers are literally called advocates.

gre.s: A longtime ____ of renewable energy, the senator surprised no one when she championed the solar subsidy bill.
gre.clue: surprised no one when she championed

example: As an advocate of cycle lanes, the young city planner rode to every council meeting on her battered bicycle.

en: Having to do with beauty and how people appreciate it
hook: AESTHETIC: think 'A STYLISH thing', all about beauty.
story: Aesthetic. Lamia's study room used to be a mess of papers and dirty cups. One weekend she changed everything: fairy lights along the shelf, a small green plant, books lined up by colour, and a soft pastel wall. Her friends gasped when they video-called her. "It is so aesthetic!" Aesthetic means concerned with beauty and artistic taste. Architects weigh function against aesthetics. Do not confuse it with ascetic, which means rejecting pleasure and comfort.

gre.s: Although the bridge is structurally sound, critics fault its ____ shortcomings, calling it the ugliest structure in the city.
gre.clue: calling it the ugliest structure in the city

example: The museum chose the old textile mill for aesthetic reasons as well as practical ones, admiring its brick arches and tall windows.

en: To stop happening or stop doing something
hook: CEASE: CEASE-FIRE, stop shooting.
story: Cease. For three days, construction drills roared outside the hostel from dawn to midnight, and students could not study for their exams. Finally the city authorities issued an order: all work must cease after eight in the evening. That night, at exactly eight, the noise stopped, and the whole hostel cheered. To cease is to come to an end, or to bring something to an end. A ceasefire is when guns stop firing. Something that never stops is unceasing. Synonyms: stop, halt.

gre.s: The two factions agreed to ____ hostilities during the festival, but the fragile truce collapsed only days after the celebrations ended.
gre.clue: the fragile truce

example: The factory ceased production in 2019, and its empty sheds now shelter stray dogs and the occasional film crew.

en: A group of similar things close together; to gather in a group
hook: CLUSTER: like a bunch of grapes clustered together.
story: Cluster. On a winter night in a village in Panchagarh, Tania looked up and found the Pleiades, which her grandmother called Krittika: seven bright stars bunched together in one small patch of sky. Below, the village children clustered around a fire to keep warm. A cluster is a group of similar things close together, and to cluster is to gather into such a group. Grapes grow in clusters, and factories often cluster near a port. Synonyms: bunch, group, huddle.

gre.s: Rather than being evenly distributed across the country, the new technology firms tend to ____ in a few urban centers, where investors and skilled engineers are concentrated.
gre.clue: Rather than being evenly distributed across the country

example: On cold winter mornings in Rangpur, rickshaw pullers cluster around the tea stalls, warming their hands on clay cups.

en: To invent a term or expression that did not exist before
hook: GRE trick: to COIN a word is to MINT a brand-new one, like a new coin.
story: Coin. Tasnim's little brother invented a word for the panic students feel the night before exam results: resultitis. Within a month, the whole hostel was using it. He had coined a new word: invented it. Writers and scientists coin terms all the time. Shakespeare is credited with coining hundreds of words, and selfie was coined only recently. Picture a mint stamping out shiny new coins: coining a phrase stamps out something new. Synonyms: invent, devise, originate.

gre.s: Rather than borrow an existing term, the psychologist decided to ____ a new one, since no word in the language captured the phenomenon she had discovered.
gre.clue: no word in the language captured the phenomenon

example: Richard Owen, the anatomist who coined the word dinosaur, built it from Greek roots meaning terrible lizard.

en: Hard to ignore because it is so interesting or convincing
hook: COMPELLING: it COMPELS, or forces, you to pay attention.
story: Compelling. Arif told himself, "Just one episode, then sleep." The new detective series opened with a murder on a ferry. Then a twist. Then a cliffhanger. At four in the morning, he was still watching, eyes burning, unable to stop. The story was compelling: so powerfully interesting that it forced him to keep going. Compelling also means convincing: compelling evidence persuades a jury. Either way, a compelling thing compels you, pushing you to pay attention.

gre.s: Although the evidence for the hypothesis was once considered thin, the new fossil discoveries make a ____ case for it.
gre.clue: Although the evidence for the hypothesis was once considered thin

example: The defense lawyer offered a compelling alibi, backed by bus tickets and a shopkeeper who remembered serving her client that night.

en: To act according to a rule, request, or command
hook: COMPLY: COMPLETE what's asked.
story: Comply. The new law said that every bus must have a speed limiter and that drivers must rest after six hours. Most transport companies complied within a month, installing the devices and changing shifts. Three companies ignored the law and were fined heavily. To comply is to act according to a rule, request, or command. Compliance with safety rules keeps everyone alive. Think: complete what was asked.

gre.s: Companies that refuse to ____ with the new environmental regulations will face heavy fines and possible closure.
gre.clue: will face heavy fines and possible closure

example: Passengers who refused to comply with the mask rule were politely asked to leave the train at the next station.

en: To make a problem worse
hook: GRE trick: COMPOUND interest grows; a COMPOUNDED problem grows worse.
story: Compound. Zayan dented his father's car in a minor bump. Instead of confessing, he hid the damage and later blamed a rickshaw. When the truth came out a week later, his father was far angrier about the lie than about the dent. Zayan had compounded his mistake: made a bad situation worse. In GRE English, to compound a problem means to add to it, just as compound interest piles interest on top of interest. Synonyms: aggravate, exacerbate, worsen.

gre.s: The governor's initial delay in ordering an evacuation was a serious error, but her subsequent refusal to admit it served only to ____ the damage to her reputation.
gre.clue: her subsequent refusal to admit it

example: A dropped catch in the final over compounded the bowler's misery, and his team lost the match by a single run.

en: To settle differences by mutual give and take; also, to weaken or endanger
bn: আপস করা; ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত বা দুর্বল করা
hook: GRE trick: COMPROMISE also means to WEAKEN — a compromised password.
story: Compromise. Rafi wanted pizza for dinner. His sister wanted biryani. After ten minutes of arguing, their mother announced a compromise: pizza tonight, biryani tomorrow. Both agreed. Later that week, Rafi shared his email password with a stranger who promised free mobile data. The next day, his account was compromised: hacked and exposed. Compromise means to settle by meeting halfway, but also to weaken or endanger something. The GRE tests both meanings.

gre.s: Engineers warned that cutting corners on materials would ____ the structural integrity of the bridge, putting thousands of commuters at risk.
gre.clue: putting thousands of commuters at risk

example: Sharing your password with a friend can compromise the security of every account linked to your email address.

en: Broad agreement shared by most or all members of a group
hook: CONSENSUS: everyone gives their CONSENT.
story: Consensus. The family had argued for an hour about the winter holiday. Cox's Bazar or Sylhet? The beach or the tea gardens? Grandma wanted hills, the kids wanted the sea, and Uncle wanted to stay home. Finally, after much tea and many compromises, everyone agreed: Cox's Bazar, with one day in the hills on the way. They had reached a consensus: general agreement among a group. Scientific consensus on climate change is overwhelming.

gre.s: Although a few dissenters remain, the scientific ____ is that human activity is the primary driver of recent warming.
gre.clue: Although a few dissenters remain

example: After two long evenings of debate, the residents of the Mirpur building reached a consensus to paint the stairwell bright yellow.

en: A firmly held belief; also, a formal declaration of guilt
hook: CONVICTION: you're CONVINCED.
story: Conviction. Tania's grandmother was the first woman in her village to send her daughters to college. Neighbours mocked her, relatives warned her, and money was always short. But she never wavered; she was certain that education would change her family. She acted from deep conviction: a firmly held belief. The word has a second meaning, a formal declaration that someone is guilty of a crime. Convict and convince share its root. Synonyms: belief, certainty, resolve.

gre.s: Though the young activist spoke softly, she argued with such ____ that even her skeptical audience could not doubt she believed every word.
gre.clue: could not doubt she believed every word

example: The old ferry captain told his passengers with quiet conviction that the storm would pass before they reached Barisal.

en: Cut off from something, with no real link to it
hook: GRE trick: DIVORCED FROM reality means disconnected from it.
story: Divorced. During a flood, a minister appeared on TV in a pressed suit and announced that the country had never been more prosperous and that every citizen was well fed. Outside the studio, thousands of people stood in line for a single bag of rice. His speech was completely divorced from reality. On the GRE, divorced from means separated from or disconnected from something. A theory divorced from evidence is just a guess.

gre.s: Critics charged that the economist's elegant models were ____ from reality, ignoring how actual consumers behave.
gre.clue: ignoring how actual consumers behave

example: Raised in a gated compound with a driver and a cook, the diplomat's children grew up divorced from ordinary life in the city.

en: Detailed and complicated (adj.); to explain in more detail (verb)
hook: E-LABOR-ATE: lots of LABOR went into it.
story: Elaborate. For her sister's holud ceremony, Ishita designed an elaborate stage: marigold garlands, hundreds of tiny lights, hand-painted winnowing trays, and a swing covered in jasmine. It took four days to build. Elaborate means detailed and complicated, made with great care. As a verb, it means to explain in more detail; when the professor says, "Please elaborate," he wants more. Notice the word labor hidden inside: lots of work. Synonyms: intricate, ornate, detailed.

gre.s: Far from the simple sketch the client had requested, the architect produced a highly ____ design, crowded with ornament and dozens of interlocking spaces.
gre.clue: Far from the simple sketch the client had requested

example: The thief's elaborate plan involved a fake delivery van, two disguises, and a tunnel dug under the jeweller's back wall.

en: To give information to; also, to give an essential quality to or influence
bn: জানানো; প্রভাবিত করা, বৈশিষ্ট্য দান করা
hook: GRE trick: experience INFORMS art means it SHAPES it from within.
story: Inform. Priya grew up in a fishing village near the Sundarbans, watching her father mend nets and survive cyclones. Years later, as an architect, she designed storm shelters for coastal towns. Every drawing carried what she had learned as a child about wind, water, and fear. Her childhood informed her work: it gave the work its essential quality and shaped it. Usually inform means to tell. On the GRE, it often means to shape or permeate, as in faith informs her poetry.

gre.s: Her years as a war correspondent continue to ____ her fiction: nearly every novel she writes returns to scenes of conflict and displacement.
gre.clue: nearly every novel she writes returns to scenes of conflict and displacement

example: Her childhood among the weavers of Tangail informs every pattern the designer creates, from silk scarves to hotel carpets.

en: To suggest or hint indirectly
hook: GRE trick: as a verb, INTIMATE means to hint, like whispering an intimate secret.
story: Intimate. Arif's manager never said, "You will be promoted." Instead, she said things like, "You may want to start thinking about how you would lead a team," and, "Next year will bring bigger responsibilities." Arif understood perfectly. She was intimating it: hinting, suggesting indirectly. As a verb, intimate means to communicate something delicately, without saying it outright. As an adjective, intimate means close and personal, as in an intimate friendship. Same spelling, different pronunciation.

gre.s: Though she never stated it outright, the minister seemed to ____ that the government would soon change its policy.
gre.clue: Though she never stated it outright

example: The landlord intimated that the rent might rise next year, though he refused to name a figure.

en: Sharp and highly developed; eager
hook: KEEN: a KEEN knife is sharp; a keen student is eager.
story: Keen. Tania's grandmother is eighty, but her eyesight is keen: she can spot a single stone in a plate of rice from across the room. Her mind is just as sharp. Tania, meanwhile, is keen to learn her grandmother's recipes and eager to start before the next family wedding. So keen means sharp and highly developed, as in a keen sense of smell, and also eager, as in keen to help. A keen blade is a sharp one. Synonyms: sharp, acute; or eager, avid.

gre.s: Her ____ eye for detail made her an invaluable editor; she routinely caught errors that had slipped past three previous readers.
gre.clue: caught errors that had slipped past three previous readers

example: A keen sense of smell lets trained airport dogs detect explosives hidden inside sealed suitcases.

en: A drawback that holds someone back; also, legal responsibility for something
hook: LIABILITY: something you're LIABLE for, a burden.
story: Liability. Farhan was the fastest bowler on his university team, but he also argued with umpires in almost every match. Twice the team was penalised, and once they nearly lost a final because he was suspended. The captain finally told him, 'Your temper is a liability.' A liability is something that puts you at a disadvantage. In law and accounting, liability also means legal responsibility, or a debt. Its opposite is an asset. Synonyms: burden, handicap, drawback.

gre.s: His reckless remarks to the press, once dismissed as charming, had become a serious ____ for the campaign, costing it the support of several key donors.
gre.clue: costing it the support of several key donors

example: In the summer heat, the team's ageing goalkeeper became a liability, too tired by the second half to dive for anything.

en: Humble about one's achievements; moderate in size or amount
hook: MODEST: MODERATE, not boastful, not extreme.
story: Modest. Nadia scored in the top one percent on her GRE. When relatives praised her at dinner, she only said she had been lucky with the reading passages, and changed the subject to her cousin's wedding. She was modest: humble about her achievements. Modest also means moderate in size or amount: a modest salary, a modest flat, a modest improvement. On the GRE, watch for this second sense. Opposites: boastful for people, and substantial or lavish for amounts.

gre.s: Despite the company's grand promises of transformation, the new policy produced only ____ gains, raising productivity by barely two percent.
gre.clue: raising productivity by barely two percent

example: The bakery started with a modest budget of fifty thousand taka and one secondhand oven in a Mohammadpur garage.

en: Biased in favor of one side; also, incomplete
hook: PARTIAL: takes PART of one side, or is only a PART.
story: Partial. In the local cricket final, every close call went to the home team. Every appeal by the visitors was rejected. The visiting captain finally complained: "The umpire is partial!" That same afternoon, the scoreboard showed only partial results because of a power cut. Partial has two meanings: biased in favour of one side, or incomplete. "I am partial to mango juice" means you especially like it.

gre.s: Because the judge's brother was a shareholder in the company, critics argued that she would inevitably be ____ in its favor and should withdraw from the case.
gre.clue: the judge's brother was a shareholder

example: A historian who is partial to one dynasty may quietly ignore records that show its rulers in a poor light.

en: Letting things happen without acting, reacting or resisting
hook: PASSIVE: lets everything PASS by without acting.
story: Passive. In group discussions, Tania sits quietly while louder classmates take over. When someone presents her idea as his own, she says nothing. When her group skips its share of the work, she does it all herself, without protest. Tania is passive: accepting what happens without active response or resistance. The word comes from the Latin pati, to suffer or endure, as in patient. Its opposite is active or assertive. Synonyms: submissive, acquiescent, inert.

gre.s: Far from being ____ spectators of the reforms, the village women organized committees, petitioned officials, and ultimately shaped how the new laws were enforced.
gre.clue: the village women organized committees, petitioned officials

example: A passive investor simply buys a fund that tracks the whole market and then leaves it alone for decades.

en: Obvious and clearly visible
hook: GRE trick: PATENT (adj.) means obvious — a patent lie is obvious to everyone.
story: Patent. Little Babu was asked if he had eaten the chocolate cake meant for the guests. "No, Ammu!" he said firmly, with chocolate smeared across his mouth, his cheeks, and the front of his shirt. His mother burst out laughing. It was a patent lie: obvious to everyone. On the GRE, patent as an adjective usually means obvious and clearly visible, not the legal right to an invention. Patently false means clearly false.

gre.s: The witness's claim was ____ false, contradicted by video footage that showed him miles away at the time.
gre.clue: contradicted by video footage

example: The company's claim that its biscuits were sugar-free was a patent lie, since sugar appeared second on the ingredients list.

en: Narrow-minded and unsophisticated
hook: PROVINCIAL: from a small PROVINCE, never seen the world.
story: Provincial. When Rafi's uncle visited Dhaka for the first time, he refused to try any food except rice and fish, laughed at people wearing jeans, and called every new idea "city nonsense." At a museum, he walked out after five minutes, saying old pots were a waste of money. His attitude was provincial: narrow-minded and unsophisticated, limited to a small place's outlook. Synonyms: insular, parochial. Its opposite is cosmopolitan.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the novelist's early work as ____, concerned only with the petty gossip of her small hometown.
gre.clue: concerned only with the petty gossip of her small hometown

example: Living abroad cured Sabrina of her provincial belief that no cuisine in the world could match her mother's cooking.

en: Guided by clear thinking and good sense rather than emotion
hook: RATIONAL: uses RATIO, measured reasoning.
story: Rational. Sara was terrified of flying. On her first flight to Malaysia, her hands shook. So she reminded herself of the rational facts: planes are statistically far safer than the Dhaka buses she takes every day, and pilots train for thousands of hours. Slowly, logic calmed her fear. Rational means based on reason or logic rather than emotion. A rational decision weighs evidence carefully. Think of a ratio: carefully measured reasoning.

gre.s: Although investors like to think of themselves as ____, studies show that their decisions are frequently driven by fear and herd behavior.
gre.clue: frequently driven by fear and herd behavior

example: Faced with a sudden fire alarm, the rational response is to leave calmly by the stairs, not to rush for the lift.

en: Firm determination; to decide firmly or settle
hook: RESOLVE: a RESOLUTION you stick to.
story: Resolve. After Tanvir failed the bar council exam twice, his friends told him to give up. Instead, he moved into a tiny room near the library, studied ten hours a day, and turned down every wedding invitation for a year. His resolve never weakened: his firm determination. He passed with distinction. As a verb, to resolve means to decide firmly, or to settle a problem, as in resolving a dispute. Synonyms: determination, tenacity, grit.

gre.s: Repeated setbacks only strengthened the climbers' ____: after each failed attempt on the summit, they returned the following season eager to try again.
gre.clue: eager to try again

example: Rumana's resolve never wavered during the long rehabilitation, and she was back on the hockey field within a year of her injury.

en: Highly developed and complex; having refined, worldly taste
hook: SOPHISTICATED: from SOPHIA, wisdom; refined and advanced.
story: Sophisticated. Imran's new phone can unlock using his face in total darkness, translate speech in real time, and identify plants from a photo. The software inside is extraordinarily sophisticated. Its designer is a sophisticated woman too: she has lived in four countries, collects modern art, and speaks five languages. Sophisticated means highly developed and complex, or worldly and refined. Sophia means wisdom.

gre.s: The fraud was so ____, involving dozens of shell companies across several countries, that investigators needed years to untangle it.
gre.clue: involving dozens of shell companies across several countries

example: Ancient Egyptian farmers developed a sophisticated network of canals and basins to spread the Nile's floodwater across their fields.

en: So delicate or precise as to be hard to notice or analyze
hook: SUBTLE: silent 'b', just as subtle as the word itself.
story: Subtle. On a GRE question, Arif narrowed his choice to two answers. They looked identical. He read them again, slowly. One said the effect was "often" observed; the other said "always." That single word made one answer correct and the other wrong. The difference was subtle: delicate, hard to notice without close attention. A subtle hint, a subtle flavour, a subtle change in tone. Even the b in subtle is silent and subtle.

gre.s: The difference between the two dialects is ____, detectable only to native speakers who have lived in both regions.
gre.clue: detectable only to native speakers

example: A skilled tea taster can detect subtle differences between leaves picked in the same Sylhet garden only a week apart.

en: Completely and absolutely
hook: UTTERLY: so complete you can't UTTER anything more.
story: Utterly. After a twenty-hour shift during the dengue outbreak, Dr. Tania walked out of the hospital utterly exhausted. Not tired. Not sleepy. Completely, totally drained. She sat down on the bus, closed her eyes for one second, and woke up at the last stop, an hour past her home. Utterly means completely and absolutely, to the fullest degree. Utterly ridiculous, utterly beautiful, utterly destroyed. It intensifies the word that follows.

gre.s: The expedition's plan, which had seemed flawless on paper, proved ____ unworkable: not a single stage could be carried out once the team reached the frozen pass.
gre.clue: not a single stage could be carried out

example: The old map proved utterly useless, since the river had shifted its course nearly a mile since it was drawn.

en: To produce or provide; to give way under pressure
hook: YIELD has two meanings: PRODUCE (a crop yields rice) and GIVE WAY (a yield sign).
story: Yield. In a northern village, farmers tried a new variety of rice developed by agricultural scientists. At harvest time, each field yielded nearly twice as much grain as before: it produced more. The amount produced is also called the yield. But yield has a second meaning: to give way under pressure. Drivers yield to an ambulance, letting it pass, and an old bridge may yield under a heavy truck. Synonyms: produce, give way, surrender.

gre.s: Researchers hoped the new irrigation method would ____ larger harvests, but in its first season the farms brought in less rice than ever.
gre.clue: but in its first season the farms brought in less rice than ever

example: The survey of three thousand households yielded surprising data on how much families spend on mobile phone credit.
